directions: Press the dust-fine seed onto the soil surface without covering, since light aids germination, and start indoors about six weeks before the last frost or direct-sow outdoors once frost danger has passed. This tough, silvery-leaved native spreads slowly by rhizome in lean, well-drained soil and shrugs off drought once established, making it a good fit for meadow and gravel gardens. It is a primary caterpillar host for the American Lady butterfly, which wraps silk-and-leaf shelters around the felted foliage, and the dried, papery flower clusters give the plant its "everlasting" reputation for cut-flower use.

planting.note: Divide clumps or set out nursery plugs in spring into consistently moist to wet, rich soil along pond edges, ditches, or rain gardens; unlike true nettles, its leaves carry no stinging hairs.

directions: Divide clumps or set out nursery plugs in spring into consistently moist to wet, rich soil along pond edges, ditches, or rain gardens; unlike true nettles, its leaves carry no stinging hairs, so it is safe to handle and site near paths. It quietly colonizes damp shade by rhizome and inconspicuous green flower spikes, functioning more as habitat infrastructure than a showpiece. Because it lacks the toxic aphids and chemistry of true stinging nettle, gardeners plant it as a safe host for Red Admiral, Eastern Comma, and Question Mark caterpillars, all of which will readily switch to it where wild nettle is scarce.

planting.note: Sow seed directly where it is to grow in fall, since the long, carrot-like taproot resents transplanting once established; seed needs roughly 60-90 days of natural winter chilling to break dormancy.

directions: Sow seed directly where it is to grow in fall, since the long, carrot-like taproot resents transplanting once established; the seed needs roughly 60-90 days of natural cold-moist winter chilling to break dormancy and sprout the following spring. This is a classic dry-slope wildflower of the interior Pacific Northwest, thriving in gravelly or rocky soils with excellent drainage and almost no summer water. Its finely divided foliage emerges very early in spring and serves as a key larval host for the Anise Swallowtail and, in rockier habitats, the Indra Swallowtail.

planting.note: Nick or hot-water-soak the hard-coated seed before sowing to mimic the fire scarification this chaparral pioneer needs in the wild, and plant in fall so seedlings establish with winter rain.

It grows quickly into an airy, broom-like subshrub on lean, disturbed, or sandy soils and fixes nitrogen, which makes it a favorite for post-fire restoration and slope stabilization in California gardens. Few plants support as many small butterfly caterpillars at once: it is a documented larval host for the Acmon Blue, Bramble Hairstreak, Silvery Blue, and Funereal Duskywing.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Divide established mats or root short stem cuttings in spring and set into sharply drained, gritty soil; resents winter wet more than cold.

directions: Divide established mats or root short stem cuttings in spring and set into sharply drained, gritty soil; this small succulent is naturally found on rocky alpine and subalpine slopes and resents winter wet more than cold. It forms a low, fleshy-leaved groundcover with bright yellow summer flowers, ideal for rock gardens, troughs, and scree plantings at elevation. It is the primary larval host of the Rocky Mountain Parnassian butterfly, whose caterpillars feed on the succulent foliage in high-elevation meadows.
